lead.title: Private chefs now command up to USD 300,000, and the household kitchen becomes the most contested hire of all
lead.standfirst: The salary for a principal's private chef has climbed to figures once reserved for the estate manager, as the wealthy chase their own Michelin standard behind closed doors.
lead.body:
The private kitchen has quietly become the front line in the war for household talent. Benchmark pay for a full-time private chef now sits around USD 150,000 at the market median, according to recruiters, with Michelin-trained candidates who travel with the family reaching USD 270,000 and beyond. In the United States the very top of the range has touched USD 300,000, a figure that would once have belonged to the person running the entire estate rather than the person running the stove.

The pressure is structural, not seasonal. The population of ultra-high-net-worth individuals keeps expanding, the pool of genuinely qualified senior candidates grows slowly, and low-tax jurisdictions led by Dubai are bidding hard for the same English-speaking talent. A principal who wants a chef able to cook at restaurant level, cater a shooting weekend, feed the children something wholesome and then plate a private dinner for twenty is competing against every other principal who wants exactly that. When supply is thin, the price of the rare candidate rises, and it has.

The consequence inside the house is a churn the sector calls job-hopping. Chefs move for a better package, a lighter travel schedule or a kinder principal, and the household that loses one is thrown back into a market where the best people are rarely available and never cheap. For the family, a chef is no longer a line item but a retention project, managed with the same care once reserved for a chief investment officer.

For those entering private service, the shift is instructive. The kitchen is now a career with a ceiling that rivals the most senior roles in the house, and the skills that command the premium are specific: formal training, discretion, the flexibility to travel at short notice and the temperament to cook for the same discerning palate every single day.
lead.why: The person who runs a principal's household must now recruit, pay and retain a chef against a market that treats the role as a six-figure career, and understand that the kitchen is as hard to staff as any seat in the house.

articles.title: The family office stops writing cheques to funds and starts doing the deals itself, and the household it runs must keep pace
articles.body:
There are now more than 8,000 family offices in the world, managing an estimated USD 5.5 trillion, a figure projected to reach USD 9 trillion by 2030. The striking change is not the size of the pool but how it is being deployed. According to the 2026 Global Family Office Report from J.P. Morgan Private Bank and parallel surveys, private markets have become the single largest allocation in the average family-office portfolio at roughly 29 per cent, ahead of public equities, fixed income, real estate and cash.

Behind that number sits a change in behaviour. Around 70 per cent of family offices now invest directly into companies rather than through funds, and roughly 83 per cent of those direct deals are done as co-investments alongside a trusted partner rather than as solo bets. The family is no longer content to be a passive holder of fund units paying two and twenty. It wants ownership, board seats and the ability to use its own expertise, and it is building the in-house teams to do so.

That ambition has a staffing consequence that reaches all the way to the front door. A family office that runs its own deals needs analysts, lawyers and operators, and it needs a principal whose time is protected so that the deals get done. The household, the aircraft, the properties and the calendar exist to buy that time back. When the office turns itself into a private investment firm, the pressure on the people who run the private life rises in step.

For the future house or estate manager, the lesson is that the family office is the true employer behind the household, and its priorities set the weather. Understanding that the principal is increasingly an operator and not merely an owner explains why discretion, speed and seamless logistics have never been more valuable.
articles.why: The family office is the institution that pays for and directs the household, and its move into hands-on dealmaking raises the premium on staff who can protect the principal's time and run the private life without friction.
articles.src: J.P. Morgan Private Bank, 2026 Global Family Office Report

articles.title: The yacht is finished but the crew is not found, and the shortage at sea now decides which boats actually sail
articles.body:
The constraint on the water in 2026 is not steel but people. Crew salaries have risen by roughly 8 to 12 per cent since 2023, pushed up by inflation and by a persistent shortage of qualified hands, and owners are being told to pay at the top of every range simply to attract and keep experienced professionals. Entry-level deckhands start around 2,500 euros a month, while a superyacht captain on a large hull can command 25,000 euros a month or more.

The scarcity is sharpest in the roles that keep a modern yacht legal and safe: engineers, qualified deck officers and crew willing to work rotational contracts that let them keep a life ashore. As the fleet grows and hulls get larger and more technical, the number of people certified to run them has not kept pace. The result is a seller's market for talent, in which the best chief stewardess or engineer can choose the boat, the itinerary and the package.

Monaco sits at the centre of this world, its calendar of the Grand Prix, the nearby Cannes festival and the autumn yacht show setting the rhythm of hiring and the premium on rates across the Mediterranean. A crew placed for a Riviera summer costs more than the same crew in a quieter market, and owners increasingly plan their recruitment around these fixed points in the year.

For the household that oversees a yacht as one asset among several, the crew shortage is a management problem as much as a maritime one. The estate manager or family office that charters or owns must now think about retention at sea in the same terms it uses ashore, because a boat without a full, qualified crew is an expensive ornament that cannot leave the quay.
articles.why: A yacht is one of the household's most complex assets, and the person who oversees it must now recruit and retain scarce, expensive crew with the same rigour applied to staff on land.
articles.src: Morgan & Mallet International, Yacht Crew Salary Guide 2026

articles.title: Two casks from a distillery that no longer exists sell for GBP 4.25 million, and the ghost of Karuizawa sets a record
articles.body:
At a Christie's wine and spirits sale in London on 10 March, two full casks of whisky from the closed Japanese distillery Karuizawa became the highest-value lots ever sold by the department, together achieving 4.25 million pounds. Each cask, numbered 6195 and 888, made 2.125 million pounds, and each holds roughly 420 bottles, giving the buyer not only the whisky but the right to shape its final maturation and release.

Karuizawa is the most storied name in Japanese whisky precisely because it is gone. Founded in 1955 in the country's Southern Alps, the distillery closed its doors in 2000, and its remaining casks were acquired for posterity only when the site was threatened with demolition a decade later. Both casks in the sale were distilled in 1999, the year before production ceased, and came from the private collection of Sukhinder Singh, one of the most respected figures in the rare-whisky world.

The result confirms a market that has moved from bottles to whole casks, and from Scotch alone to a global chase that now runs through Japan and, separately, the United States. It is a market driven by scarcity in its purest form: a distillery that can never make another drop, and a finite number of casks that will only diminish as they are bottled.

For anyone serving a collector, fluency in this world is now part of the craft. Sourcing, storage, provenance and the quiet etiquette of the auction room are the concierge's domain, and a name like Karuizawa is exactly the kind of cultural knowledge a principal expects the household to possess before it is ever asked for.
articles.why: Collections of this kind pass through the household's hands, and cultural fluency in wine, whisky and provenance is part of the service a discerning principal takes for granted.

articles.title: Aman prepares its first Maldives island inside a protected biosphere, and the private escape learns to answer to the reef
articles.body:
Aman has confirmed its first property in the Maldives, on an island that sits inside the UNESCO Biosphere Reserve of Baa Atoll, close to the celebrated manta and whale-shark waters of Hanifaru Bay. The plan runs to roughly 35 pavilions and villas, each with its own pool, alongside an Aman Spa and a resident marine-biology programme, a scale that is deliberately small for a brand that trades on space and silence.

The choice of a protected reserve is the point. Placing a resort inside a biosphere binds the operator to the health of the reef and the seasons of the marine life around it, and turns conservation from a marketing line into an operating constraint. For the guest who has seen every over-water villa, the promise is access to a genuinely protected marine environment rather than another manufactured lagoon.

Maldives openings are famously prone to slippage, and several rival debuts have already moved into 2027, so the date should be read as an intention rather than a fixture. What is not in doubt is the direction of the ultra-luxury market, which continues to reward privacy, small key counts and a credible environmental story over sheer scale.

For the household that plans a family's travel, an opening like this is a note for the file. It signals where the most private guests will want to be, the kind of advance access that will need to be secured, and the growing expectation that even a barefoot escape now comes wrapped in a conservation commitment the principal will want honoured.
articles.why: Planning private travel means knowing which openings the most discreet families will chase, and increasingly that a destination's environmental credentials are part of what the principal expects the household to have vetted.

briefs.b: The Henley Private Wealth Migration Report 2026 forecasts that as many as 165,000 millionaires will relocate internationally this year, up from about 142,000 in 2025 and the highest intensity recorded in 15 years. The United Arab Emirates remains the leading destination, while Singapore tops the report's new competitiveness score at 79.5 out of 100.

Recruiters report that house manager is now the fastest-rising salary among household staff, with average pay around USD 86,000 and the estate-manager range running from roughly USD 85,000 to USD 250,000. A slow-growing pool of qualified candidates and competition from Dubai continue to push senior pay to record levels.

Sotheby's sold what it called the most valuable single-owner American whiskey collection ever offered at auction, totalling USD 2.5 million. Highlights included an Old Rip Van Winkle 20 Years Old, a sign that the rare-spirits chase now runs as strongly through American bourbon as through Scotch and Japanese malt.

lead.title: The chief of staff rises above the household, and the family now pays a private executive to run the whole life
lead.standfirst: As fortunes grow more complex, the wealthiest houses are hiring a single senior professional to sit above the estate and command it, at pay that now rivals a corporate director.
lead.body:
For most of its history the private household answered to a butler or, in the grand American manner, an estate manager. In 2026 a new title sits above both. The chief of staff has become the most senior seat in private service, a role modelled less on the pantry than on the corner office, and the salary guides that track this world now place it at the very top of the pay scale.

The numbers are striking. Recruiters specialising in ultra-high-net-worth households put chief of staff compensation from USD 180,000 to more than USD 250,000 a year, frequently before housing, a vehicle and performance bonuses are counted. In the deepest markets the figure runs to USD 300,000, while the same title in France might command little more than a fifth of that, a gap that tells you where the demand truly sits. The United States now dominates the search for these professionals, with the role ranking among the five most requested positions in the American private market.

What the family is buying is not a housekeeper with a grander name. The modern chief of staff is a direct adviser to the principal who manages global operations across several homes, oversees the estate managers and personal assistants beneath, and often works alongside the family office on budgets, contracts and staff of their own. Where the estate manager runs a property, the chief of staff runs a life: the diary, the households, the aircraft and the people who serve them, reporting to the principal much as a chief executive reports to a board.

The rise of the role is a direct consequence of scale. A family that owns four residences on three continents, charters or owns aircraft, and employs twenty or thirty people cannot be run from the kitchen table, and the principals rarely wish to run it themselves. Recruiters describe a market where senior pay has climbed through 2025 and into 2026, pushed by an expanding wealthy base, a candidate pool that grows slowly, and low-tax jurisdictions competing hard for the same English-speaking talent. The qualified chief of staff can now name terms.

For anyone training to serve at the top of a private household, the lesson is that the ceiling has risen. The path no longer ends at butler or house manager; it can lead to a seat that commands the entire operation and is paid accordingly. But the skills that carry a candidate there are as much managerial as domestic, and the family that hires a chief of staff is, in the end, buying judgement.
lead.why: For the student of private service, the chief of staff marks the point where a domestic career becomes an executive one, and where discretion, management and financial literacy matter as much as the traditional service crafts.
lead.src: Morgan & Mallet International; Oplu Private Staff Salary Guide 2026

articles.title: The family office spreads across the world, and for the first time Asia keeps more of them than Europe
articles.body:
The private institution that sits behind the great fortunes is multiplying faster than at any point in its history. Deloitte's latest global count puts the number of single family offices at 8,030 as of 2024, a rise of 31 per cent from 6,130 in 2019, and projects the figure will pass 10,000 before the decade is out. The assets they steward are climbing with them, from an estimated USD 3.1 trillion today towards USD 5.4 trillion by 2030.

The more telling shift is where these offices now sit. North America still leads with roughly 3,180, but Asia-Pacific has, for the first time, overtaken Europe, with about 2,290 offices against Europe's 2,020. Deloitte expects North America to nearly double its count by 2030 while Asia-Pacific grows fastest of all, a rebalancing that follows the new money being made across the Gulf and the East.

A family office is, in plain terms, the private company a family builds to manage its wealth, its property, its philanthropy and often its staff. Some run investments alone; many now run the whole apparatus of a wealthy life, employing the accountants, lawyers, security and household principals who once reported directly to the family. As the number of offices grows, so does their appetite for people.

That appetite reaches directly into the world of private service. The household staff, the estate manager and increasingly the chief of staff sit within or alongside the family office, and the professionalisation the offices bring, with budgets, contracts and reporting lines, is reshaping how domestic work is hired and paid. The wealth that once ran on trust and habit now runs on structure.
articles.why: The family office is becoming the employer of record for private service, and the student who understands how it works, where it is growing, and who it answers to, understands where the jobs and the money are moving.
articles.src: Deloitte Private, Family Office Insights Series

articles.title: American wealth goes looking for a second home abroad, and the map of where the rich settle is redrawn
articles.body:
The great migration of the wealthy shows no sign of slowing. Henley and Partners forecasts that as many as 165,000 millionaires will change country in 2026, the largest movement of private wealth on record and a further rise on the 142,000 who relocated in 2025. The headline number, though, hides the more interesting story beneath it.

For the first time the flow includes a marked surge of Americans seeking a foothold abroad. The firm reports affluent United States citizens pursuing international diversification in unprecedented numbers, less as an exit than as insurance, a second residence and a second passport held against uncertainty at home. At the same time the United Arab Emirates, the leading destination of the past two years, is prompting its own internationally mobile residents to think about contingencies.

Henley has also changed how it reads the market. Its 2026 report introduces a Global Wealth Mobility Framework, a model that scores jurisdictions on their structural ability to attract and hold mobile wealth rather than simply counting arrivals and departures. Singapore leads the ranking with a competitiveness score of 79.5 out of 100, confirming the pull of the Gulf and South East Asia away from the older centres of Europe and North America.

For the household, a mobile principal is a demanding one. A family that assembles a life across several countries needs staff who can move with it, open and close houses, manage visas and logistics, and keep a standard of service consistent from one jurisdiction to the next. The fortune that travels turns the household into a travelling institution.
articles.why: Wealth migration decides where private service is hired and how it is delivered, and the professional who can run a household across borders is exactly the person the mobile family is now short of.
articles.src: Henley & Partners, Private Wealth Migration Report 2026

articles.title: The fine wine market steadies at last, and Burgundy and Champagne lead the cellar back to health
articles.body:
After a long correction, the fine wine market is finding its feet. The Liv-ex indices have steadied through 2026 and the auction rooms are once again clearing their lots, a sign that collectors are buying rather than merely watching. The recovery is uneven, but it has a clear leader: Burgundy, with Champagne close behind.

The numbers from the salerooms tell the story. Sotheby's reported USD 127.5 million in wine and spirits sales for 2025, up 12 per cent on the year, with Burgundy accounting for 39 per cent of the total and Bordeaux rising to 28 per cent. The house sold 96 per cent of the lots it offered, the strongest clearance in several years, on the back of landmark sales of Domaine de la Romanee-Conti, Petrus and rare Champagne in magnum.

Analysts expect Burgundy and Champagne to appreciate further, by perhaps 8 to 12 per cent, held up by genuine scarcity and steady collector demand, while Bordeaux first growths sit stable with reliable bidding. Champagne has proved less volatile than Burgundy and more resilient than Bordeaux through the downturn, though the trade is careful to call the wider recovery tentative and patchy rather than a boom.

For the household, wine is rarely just an investment. It is a cellar to be built, insured, stored at temperature and served at the right moment, and a principal who collects at this level expects the staff around them to speak the language of the bottle. Fluency in wine is part of the service.
articles.why: A serious cellar is one of the assets a private household is trusted to manage, and the professional who can read the market, buy well and serve with confidence adds a cultural competence the wealthy notice.

articles.title: Rosewood prepares to open on the Red Sea, and a new coast is built for the family that wants to be first
articles.body:
Some destinations are found; this one is being made. Rosewood Red Sea is preparing to open within Amaala, the wellness-led district rising on Saudi Arabia's north-western coast, some 550 kilometres north of Jeddah and framed by the world's fourth-largest coral reef with the Hijazi mountains behind it.

The property will hold 110 suites and villas alongside 25 Rosewood Residences, the branded homes that let a family own rather than merely visit. It is a familiar pattern at the top of the market, where the residence attached to the hotel offers a household the service of a great property without the burden of building one from scratch.

The setting is the point. Amaala and the wider Red Sea development have been conceived for a traveller who wants somewhere new, unspoilt and exclusive, and the coral, the mountains and the deliberate remoteness are the whole proposition. For the family that likes to arrive before the crowd, a coast with no history yet is its own kind of luxury.
articles.why: The branded residence beside a new resort is exactly the kind of property a private household may soon be asked to run, and knowing how these places work is part of reading where the wealthy will next choose to be.

briefs.b: UBS puts the world's dollar millionaires at roughly 57.5 million, of whom more than 23.6 million, over 40 per cent, now live in the United States. Even as fortunes at the top swelled, median wealth fell in most countries the bank tracks, a reminder that the growth is concentrated at the very peak.

Knight Frank's latest reading has prime residential prices up 3.2 per cent across the world's leading markets in 2025, a shade below the previous year. The Middle East, led by Dubai, set the pace, with Asia-Pacific and Europe close behind.

Monterey Car Week is under way in California, building to the 75th Pebble Beach Concours d'Elegance on 16 August. The week's flagship auctions from Gooding Christie's, RM Sotheby's and Mecum run from 12 to 15 August, the year's most closely watched test of the collector-car market.

lead.title: Global wealth climbs at its fastest pace in eight years, and nearly a million new millionaires arrive to be served
lead.standfirst: The UBS Global Wealth Report 2026 records a 10.8 per cent rise in personal wealth in 2025, and the household is asked to serve a client base that is both larger and richer.
lead.body:
On 30 June UBS published the seventeenth edition of its Global Wealth Report, and the headline number was the largest in years. Global personal wealth rose by 10.8 per cent in USD terms in 2025, far ahead of the 4.6 per cent recorded in 2024 and the 4.2 per cent of 2023, and the fastest expansion since 2017. It was the third consecutive year of growth, driven by strong financial markets, rising property values and a weaker US dollar that amplified gains outside the United States.

The wealth was not spread evenly. Europe, the Middle East and Africa led with a 17.5 per cent increase, the Americas followed at 8.5 per cent and Asia-Pacific grew 5.9 per cent. Switzerland kept its place at the top of the league for average wealth per adult, at USD 910,382, ahead of the United States and Luxembourg. The number of US dollar millionaires rose 1.5 per cent, close to one million new millionaires in a single year, or more than 2,600 every day. The United States alone added over 440,000 of them.

For the household, the most telling detail sits above the millionaire line. UBS found that the tiers from USD 5 million to USD 100 million, the larger relations of the everyday millionaires who hold between USD 1 million and USD 5 million, expanded fastest of all, in both number and total wealth, with the sharpest acceleration in mainland China, Australia and the United States. This is precisely the band that hires private staff, buys second and third homes and builds a family office. A rising tide at the top means a rising number of houses that need running.

The report analysed 56 markets covering more than 92 per cent of the world's wealth, and its message for anyone entering private service is plain. The client base is not only richer but broader, and it is forming in places that held few large fortunes a decade ago. The estate that needs a manager next year may sit in Riyadh, Milan or Singapore rather than in the traditional capitals.
lead.why: A larger and faster-growing pool of wealthy households means more principals seeking trained staff, and sharper competition for the people who can run a great house.

articles.title: The butler returns to the centre of the household, and the salary now runs to six figures for the right person
articles.body:
The role many assumed had faded into period drama has, in 2026, become one of the most sought-after hires in private service. UK salary guides now place a formal butler on a range from about GBP 45,000 to GBP 80,000, while a head butler running a principal residence with staff beneath them can command from GBP 65,000 to GBP 150,000. A house manager, the modern title that often absorbs the butler's duties in a busy household, sits between GBP 75,000 and GBP 115,000 for a single significant home.

The numbers reflect scarcity rather than nostalgia. Agencies report a shrinking pool of experienced domestic professionals set against a growing number of principals willing to pay for them, and the result is that recruitment costs, hiring times and salaries have all climbed through 2025 and into 2026. The classically trained butler, fluent in service, wine, wardrobe and the choreography of a formal dinner, is rare, and the household that finds one now moves quickly to keep them.

Part of the pressure is that the job has widened. The contemporary butler is expected to manage a house's technology, its security routines and its suppliers as readily as its silver, and to move with the family between residences and time zones. Discretion, once assumed, is now written into contracts, and the ability to lead a small team has become as valued as the ability to lay a table.

For anyone training for this world, the lesson is that the ceiling has risen. The distance between an entry salary and a head-of-house salary is now measured in tens of thousands of pounds, and it is closed by exactly the skills a serious programme teaches: formal service, management, and the judgement to run a household without being told.
articles.why: The premium on trained butlers rewards precisely the formal-service and management skills a private-service education is built to deliver.
articles.src: Irving Scott Household Staff Salary Guide 2026

articles.title: Italy raises the price of its flat tax to 300,000 euros, and Milan keeps filling with the households that pay it
articles.body:
From 1 January 2026 the annual lump sum that lets a new resident of Italy shelter all foreign income from ordinary tax rose from 200,000 euros to 300,000 euros, with an additional 50,000 euros for each family member, up from 25,000 euros. The regime still runs for up to fifteen years, and even at the higher price it remains one of the most attractive propositions in Europe for a very wealthy family choosing where to live.

The increase has not slowed the movement it was designed to manage. Since Italy introduced the scheme it has drawn well over a thousand participants, and the flow accelerated after the United Kingdom abolished its non-domiciled regime, sending a wave of internationally mobile families to look for a new base. Milan has been the chief beneficiary, its property market, restaurants and business scene visibly reshaped by the arrival of big spenders from London, Switzerland and beyond.

For the household, a move of this kind is rarely just a change of address. A family that relocates to Milan or Lake Como typically rebuilds a full domestic operation on arrival, hiring or transferring an estate manager, house staff, drivers and often a family office, and doing so at speed in an unfamiliar market. The tax ruling is the beginning of the work, not the end of it.

The wider pattern matters for anyone entering service. Governments are dividing sharply into those courting the wealthy and those taxing them harder, and each policy shift redraws the map of where private staff are needed. The countries that win these households are, in effect, deciding where the next generation of great houses will be built.
articles.why: Every tax-driven relocation creates a new household to be staffed and run, and rewards the professional who can rebuild a domestic operation in a new country at short notice.

articles.title: Private jets fly more than ever in 2026, and the way families buy their flying is changing beneath the numbers
articles.body:
Business aviation had its busiest first half on record in 2026. WingX counted about 1.95 million departures worldwide in the six months to June, up 4 per cent on the same period a year earlier, with North America accounting for roughly two thirds of all activity at 1.77 million flights. Demand held up even as fuel prices rose, a sign that for the families at the top of this market flying private is a fixed habit rather than a discretionary treat.

Beneath the total, the composition of the market is shifting. Fractional operations, where a family buys a share in an aircraft and a set number of hours rather than the whole jet, grew fastest of all, climbing 11.7 per cent in North America and adding nearly 39,000 flights. At the same time corporate flight departments, the in-house fleets run by companies, contracted almost 9 per cent. The private individual, not the corporation, is now driving the growth.

Geography told its own story. North American departures rose 5 per cent and Latin America 4.6 per cent, while the Middle East fell 17.8 per cent as regional conflict disrupted flying. For a household that arranges travel, these are not abstractions: they change which aircraft are available, from where, and at what price, often at short notice during a busy season.

The move toward fractional and shared ownership also changes the concierge's task. Instead of managing one aircraft and one crew, the person arranging a principal's travel increasingly coordinates programmes, hours and providers, reading availability across a fleet rather than a single hangar. Fluency in how private aviation actually works has become part of the job description.
articles.why: As families shift from whole-aircraft ownership to fractional programmes, the value moves to the staff who can navigate providers, hours and availability on the principal's behalf.

articles.title: The pre-owned watch market grinds back to health, and the smallest watches lead the way up
articles.body:
After a long correction, the secondary market for luxury watches is recovering, quietly but steadily. Morgan Stanley's latest reading of the WatchCharts data, covering the first quarter of 2026, found 25 of the 35 brands it tracks in positive territory, with prices rising quarter on quarter at Rolex, Patek Philippe, Audemars Piguet, Cartier and Omega. The upturn has been under way since the summer of 2025 and remains gentle rather than giddy.

The gains are real over a longer view. The WatchCharts index for Patek Philippe rose about 18 per cent over the past year and the Rolex index about 9 per cent, even as both sat well below the peaks of the boom. The single sharpest trend is a change of taste. Smaller cases are back in demand, and a 35mm Patek Philippe Nautilus has risen roughly 52 per cent over two years, far ahead of the 27 per cent gain on its larger sibling.

For the household, the watch is not merely an ornament but an asset class in motion, and often one the principal collects seriously. Knowing which references are appreciating, which trade above retail and which sit below it is part of the cultural fluency a good private professional is expected to carry, alongside wine, art and cars.

The correction has also been a lesson in patience. The market that doubled and then fell has taught collectors, and those who serve them, that provenance, condition and the right reference matter more than hype. The rarest and best-kept pieces held their value through the downturn, and it is those that are leading the market back.
articles.why: A principal's watch collection is a live asset, and the professional who understands its market adds real cultural and practical value to the household.
articles.src: WatchPro, on Morgan Stanley WatchCharts data

articles.title: Rosewood prepares to open on the Via Veneto, and Rome regains a grand address for the travelling family
articles.body:
Rosewood is preparing to open its first hotel in Rome, on the Via Veneto, the boulevard that gave the world its image of Roman glamour. The property is reported to offer around 155 rooms and suites, including some fifty suites, and it joins a wave of ultra-luxury openings that has made 2026 one of the busiest years on record at the top of the hotel trade.

For the household that travels, an opening of this kind is less a holiday than a piece of infrastructure. A family passing through Rome for a season, a wedding or a business matter needs a base that can hold its staff, its security and its routines, and a new flagship on the Via Veneto offers exactly that, with the service standards a demanding principal expects.

The return of a grand name to Rome is also a signal about where wealth is spending its time. Italy's appeal to internationally mobile families, sharpened by its tax regime, is drawing them south for longer stays, and the hotels are following the money. For the concierge, one more world-class address in a favoured city is one more reliable option when a principal decides, at short notice, to be in Rome.
articles.why: A new flagship in a favoured city gives the concierge another dependable base for a principal's stay, staff and security when plans change quickly.

briefs.b: Deloitte counts around 8,030 single family offices worldwide as of 2024, up 31 per cent on 2019, managing about USD 3.1 trillion. Both figures are projected to keep climbing, to more than 10,700 offices and USD 5.4 trillion by 2030. Each new office is a professional household in miniature, and another employer of private staff.

Knight Frank recorded 636 sales of homes worth USD 10 million or more across twelve leading markets in the first quarter of 2026, up 14 per cent on the previous quarter and a one-year high. Dubai, Hong Kong and New York together took close to 60 per cent of the global total. Every such sale creates a new household to be furnished, staffed and run.

The tenth edition of Only Watch, the biennial charity auction, sold 47 unique pieces for a combined CHF 28,320,000 in aid of research into Duchenne muscular dystrophy. The sale is a reminder that at the top of collecting, rarity and philanthropy are often knocked down in the same lot.

UBS highlights the rise of the everyday millionaire, the individual holding between USD 1 million and USD 5 million, a tier that has swelled to tens of millions of people worldwide since 2000. It is the fastest-growing band of the affluent, and increasingly the household that hires its first private staff.

lead.title: The wealthy stop choosing a country and start assembling a portfolio of them, and the household must now run a life spread across borders
lead.standfirst: Henley & Partners reframes wealth migration around structural competitiveness, and finds the world's richest families increasingly holding residence, citizenship and business across several jurisdictions at once.
lead.body:
The question that has shaped a decade of wealth reporting, where are the millionaires moving, has quietly changed. In its Private Wealth Migration Report 2026, released in London on 16 June, Henley & Partners retires its headline count of how many millionaires cross borders and replaces it with a Global Wealth Mobility Framework that scores jurisdictions from zero to 100 on twelve weighted dimensions, from tax treatment and rule of law to family inclusion and geopolitical stability. The shift is telling. The firm argues that the more useful question is no longer where wealth is moving, but why, and what makes some places win it while others lose it.

The numbers behind the framework describe a class of client that no longer belongs to a single country. In the first five months of 2026 alone, Henley received applications from 86 nationalities across 47 investment migration programmes, and more than 28 per cent of applicants already lived outside their country of nationality. The firm's chief executive, Dr. Juerg Steffen, puts it plainly: for a century governments could treat their wealthiest residents as a fixed asset, rooted by business and family. That assumption, he says, is now outdated. The wealthy of 2026 build what the report calls a sovereign portfolio, residence in one country, citizenship in another, banking and business in a third.

The league table rewards stability and openness. The United Arab Emirates records one of the highest scores in the framework at 85.3, reflecting low taxation, connectivity and long residence pathways, even as regional conflict tests the Gulf. Singapore follows at 79.5 and New Zealand at 75.8, with Italy at 72.3 singled out as a European success story, its flat-tax regime for new residents drawing capital and pushing Milan forward as an international family office centre. The pressure points are just as instructive: the United Kingdom sits at 68.3 and France at 65.7, both marked down on precisely the dimensions mobile wealth weighs most heavily after a run of tax reform and fiscal uncertainty.

Two flashpoints dominate the year. The United States, the largest engine of new wealth, scores only 62.3, a paradox the report attributes to citizenship-based taxation and fiscal complexity. Applications from US nationals doubled in 2025 and remain elevated, with nearly half directed at European programmes. In Britain, foreign nationals now account for 53 per cent of applications from UK addresses, meaning British citizens make up almost half, up from just 8 per cent in 2018. As the economist Douglas McWilliams observes in the report, high-net-worth migration is the canary in the coal mine for economic policy.
lead.why: For a house manager, the principal's map is no longer a single address. A family holding residence in one country, a passport in another and a business in a third asks its staff to run a household that moves between jurisdictions, tax years and legal regimes, and to know which rules apply where.

articles.title: The estate manager becomes the household's most expensive generalist, and the family pays for the one person who can run everything at once
articles.body:
Of all the roles a modern household hires, the estate manager is the one asked to hold the whole thing together, and the market now prices that breadth accordingly. According to Lighthouse Careers, whose 2026 compensation guide was last updated on 26 July, estate managers earn base salaries from USD 120,000 to more than USD 300,000, with entry-level posts starting between USD 120,000 and USD 160,000 and senior managers of ten years or more commanding USD 200,000 to USD 300,000 and above. Once housing, benefits and bonuses are added, total packages for the top tier routinely pass USD 500,000.

Geography sets the ceiling. Monaco and the French Riviera lead at USD 250,000 to more than USD 400,000 in base pay, with Dubai close behind at USD 200,000 to USD 350,000, tax-free. The premium reflects scarcity as much as cost of living. The guide describes a market where demand exceeds the supply of qualified candidates, where base pay is rising by 8 to 12 per cent a year, and where the candidate who can combine security, technology, budgeting and staff management under one contract barely exists.

What lifts the estate manager above the other senior hires is scope. A single estate below USD 20 million in value sits at the base of the range, but a multi-property domestic portfolio adds a premium of 15 to 25 per cent, and an international portfolio from 25 to 40 per cent. Managers running budgets above USD 10 million a year, or teams of more than thirty staff, add more again. Increasingly the role is folded into the family office itself, and Lighthouse notes that family-office-integrated estate managers earn 20 to 40 per cent more than their traditional peers, with a path onward to chief of staff.

The context is a wealthy world buying more houses in more places. As families assemble the multi-jurisdiction portfolios described elsewhere in today's edition, each new address needs someone to open it, staff it, secure it and close it. The estate manager is the hinge on which that machine turns, which is why the qualified one has become the household's costliest and most contested hire.
articles.why: This is the career many students are training towards. The figures show where the value sits: not in a single specialism, but in the ability to run every part of a household, across several properties, and to speak the language of the family office.

articles.title: Forty-three new yachts converge on Port Hercule, and the boat delivered this year becomes the rarest thing on the water
articles.body:
On 17 July the Monaco Yacht Show published the first fleet list for its 35th edition, from 23 to 26 September at Port Hercule, and the headline is a study in scarcity. Of a fleet expected to reach 120 yachts by opening day, 43 will have been delivered during 2026. The organiser's chief executive, Toby Moore, frames the appeal in a single line: at a time when a new commission at a leading shipyard means waiting until 2028 or beyond, the chance to walk the decks of forty-three yachts delivering this year, in one harbour, over four days, is the most concrete thing the show offers a buyer.

The scarcity is structural. BOAT International's Global Order Book 2026 records the order book contracting in unit count for a second consecutive year, even as average length and tonnage under construction stand at record highs and build slots at the best yards are committed through 2028 and 2029. The result is that a yacht ready to sail in 2026 is among the rarest commodities in the market. The class of 2026 spans the full length of the fleet, from the 23.98 metre Arcadia A80 to the 102 metre Lurssen Nixie berthed at Quai Rainier Ier.

The densest part of the fleet sits where semi-custom production meets charter economics, in the 40 to 60 metre band, and it is dominated by this year's deliveries: Benetti's B.Now 50m, Riva's 54 Metri, Overmarine's Mangusta 165 REV and Baglietto's Fast50 and T60 among them. Italian builders account for 52 per cent of global production, and the yards of Sanlorenzo, Azimut-Benetti and the Ferretti Group brands top the hull count. Of the yachts so far confirmed, 38 are presented not by their builders but by brokerage and charter firms, an in-service fleet averaging close to 49 metres and covering every stage of ownership, from charter to management to resale.

For the people who run these vessels, the read is the same as it is ashore. New tonnage means new interiors, new systems and new crew positions to fill at a moment when qualified crew are already scarce. A yacht delivered this year is not only a rare asset to buy or charter; it is a fresh set of standards to master for the stewardess, purser or captain who steps aboard.
articles.why: The concierge and estate manager increasingly co-ordinate the family's time afloat. Knowing which yachts are new, which are for charter and why near-term availability is so tight is part of managing a principal's calendar and expectations at sea.
articles.src: Monaco Yacht Show (BOAT International Global Order Book 2026)

articles.title: The art market rebounds by seventy per cent, and the recovery reaches far below the trophy lots
articles.body:
After two lean years, the auction market has turned. According to a report from the analysts ArtTactic, published on 10 July, global auction sales at Christie's, Sotheby's and Phillips rose 70 per cent year-on-year in the first half of 2026, to USD 6.8 billion including fees, the strongest first-half performance since 2022. Christie's took USD 3.4 billion, up 71 per cent; Sotheby's USD 2.8 billion, also up 71 per cent; and Phillips USD 505.4 million, up 59 per cent.

The most important detail is not the total but its breadth. ArtTactic's founder, Anders Petterson, argues that the recovery is proving far broader than the headline results at the very top, with confidence returning to the market's middle core. Sell-through rates have risen to 91 per cent so far this year, bolstered by 131 white-glove sales where every lot found a buyer. Day sales are strong, the USD 50,000 to USD 500,000 segment is growing, and online-only auctions have climbed 22 per cent from a five-year low, with a record 33,474 lots sold online.

London led the geography, its total up 131 per cent to USD 1.42 billion, only just short of the post-pandemic high of 2022, helped by the USD 390 million sale of the Lewis collection in June. The results look baffling against a backdrop of inflation and conflict, but Petterson offers a simple explanation: many art buyers have seen their wealth rise, with the S&P 500 up around 10 per cent this year, and luxury consumption tends to follow asset prices rather than economic confidence. Someone whose portfolio has gained is unlikely to postpone a USD 5 million acquisition over weaker data.

The recovery reaches beyond fine art. Sales of luxury collectibles at the three houses rose 25 per cent, with memorabilia the standout, up 308 per cent to USD 96.1 million. Even Hong Kong, whose relative market share slipped as London, New York and Paris grew, saw its own sales volume rise almost 30 per cent to USD 764 million.
articles.why: A collection is often the most personal thing a household holds. Understanding how the market moves, where confidence sits and why a work carries the value it does is part of the cultural fluency a senior member of staff is expected to bring to the table.

articles.title: Dubai settles at the top of the world's super-prime market, and where the family buys now redraws the map of service
articles.body:
The market for the world's most expensive homes has a new capital. In the first quarter of 2026, Dubai recorded 193 super-prime residential transactions above USD 10 million, worth more than USD 3.4 billion, the highest count of any city tracked in Knight Frank's Global Super-Prime Intelligence report. Hong Kong ranked second with 94 such sales worth more than USD 1.8 billion, a 16 per cent rise in volume quarter-on-quarter, while New York came third with 90 transactions worth almost USD 1.7 billion.

Together, those three cities accounted for nearly 60 per cent of all super-prime sales across the twelve global markets Knight Frank follows, and transaction volume across the group reached a one-year peak. The surge was driven by market comebacks in Dubai, Hong Kong, New York, Palm Beach and Singapore, holding up even against higher borrowing costs and policy uncertainty. Knight Frank's head of global research, Liam Bailey, cautions that Dubai's second-quarter figures may soften, since much of the first quarter reflected deals struck before regional conflict, but the structural picture is clear: the centre of gravity in ultra-prime property has moved east and to the Gulf.

For the households that serve these buyers, the consequence is geographic. Each USD 10 million purchase is not a transaction but the birth of a household, a house that must be staffed, secured and run, often as one node in a portfolio spread across continents. The rise of Dubai as the busiest super-prime market, sitting alongside its high score for wealth mobility, means more of that service is now delivered in the Gulf, on Gulf terms, and the estate manager or concierge who understands the region carries a premium to match.
articles.why: Where the wealthy buy decides where the work is. A private household is created with every super-prime purchase, and the shift towards Dubai and Hong Kong is reshaping where staff are hired, based and paid.

articles.title: Six Senses arrives in Brera, and Milan's rise as a home for wealth gains a wellness address
articles.body:
Milan will gain one of the year's most watched hotel openings when Six Senses arrives on Via Brera in late 2026, in the heart of the city's artistic quarter. The property is modest in scale by design, with 68 rooms, of which 15 are suites and two carry their own plunge pools, and interiors by Tara Bernerd & Partners that lean on Arabescato marble, antique brass and smoked glass in a nod to Milan's standing as a design capital. A state-of-the-art spa, a sky pool and a rooftop bar anchor the wellness offer, with the Pinacoteca di Brera and the Duomo a short walk away.

The timing is not incidental. As Henley & Partners notes in today's lead, Italy has become one of Europe's clearest winners in the competition for mobile wealth, its flat-tax regime for new residents drawing entrepreneurs and investors, and Milan emerging as an international financial and family office centre. A Six Senses in Brera is the hospitality expression of that shift, a wellness-led base in a city that is quietly becoming a place the wealthy choose to live rather than merely visit.

For a private principal weighing where to spend time, or where to place a family office, a serious hotel signals a serious city. The opening gives the household a benchmark for the standard of service, spa and design its own residence in Milan will be measured against.
articles.why: Concierges and house managers are expected to know the best new addresses before their principals ask. A landmark opening in a rising wealth capital like Milan is exactly the kind of intelligence the role is built on.

briefs.b: Global business aviation activity rose 4.2 per cent in the first half of 2026, with 2.44 million departures worldwide, according to ARGUS International. North America completed 1.77 million flights, up 3.5 per cent and its best first half in four years, with fractional flying the standout at plus 11.7 per cent.

Sales of luxury collectibles at Christie's, Sotheby's and Phillips rose 25 per cent in the first half of 2026, with memorabilia up 308 per cent to USD 96.1 million. Heritage Auctions, which specialises in collectibles, posted record half-year sales of USD 1.4 billion, nearly 47 per cent above 2025.

Hong Kong recorded 94 super-prime home sales above USD 10 million in the first quarter of 2026, worth more than USD 1.8 billion, a 157 per cent jump year-on-year for houses and flats combined. Pent-up demand and limited supply drove the rebound, according to Knight Frank.

The United States is the world's largest source of new wealth yet scores only 62.3 on Henley's wealth-mobility scale, held back by citizenship-based taxation and fiscal complexity. Applications from US nationals doubled in 2025, with nearly half directed at European programmes.

lead.title: Close protection becomes the household's fastest-growing hire, and the family now budgets for safety the way it once budgeted for staff
lead.standfirst: Executive protection is the quickest-rising role in private security, and the modern household increasingly builds a discreet detail into its running costs.
lead.body:
For most of the last century the private household measured itself in visible service: the butler at the door, the chauffeur at the car, the cook in the kitchen. In 2026 a quieter figure has moved to the centre of the payroll. Close protection, once the preserve of heads of state and touring celebrities, has become the fastest-growing role in the whole of private security, and the family that lives at the top of the wealth curve now treats a personal detail as a fixed cost rather than a crisis measure.

The numbers explain the shift. Demand for close protection is rising by about 15 per cent a year, the fastest of any security discipline, and pay is climbing by roughly 9 per cent, also the quickest in the field. In the United Kingdom, an experienced officer on a private family assignment commands from 350 to 600 pounds a day, with elite hostile-environment work reaching around 110,000 pounds a year. In the United States the market is deeper still: an executive-protection detail agent sits near USD 128,000 in base pay, a detail leader near USD 185,000, and a director of security near USD 230,000. Contract day rates run from USD 1,200 to USD 2,500 an agent, depending on experience and whether the work stays at home or crosses borders.

The real cost, however, is not one person but the rota. Round-the-clock cover of a principal or a residence cannot be done by a single officer, and a three-agent rotation to hold a property twenty-four hours a day costs from USD 285,000 to USD 375,000 a year in salary alone, before travel, equipment and training. This is why protection now appears on the same ledger as the estate manager and the private chef, and why the family that adds a detail rarely does so lightly.

The bar to entry is high. Serious details expect from 5 to 10 years of experience, and the most demanding ultra-high-net-worth assignments look for at least a decade, ideally with military or specialist policing behind it. The officer is expected to be invisible in a drawing room and decisive on a pavement, to read a route as fluently as a maitre d' reads a table. That blend of discretion and capability is scarce, and scarcity, as ever in this world, is what sets the price.

For the household that surrounds the principal, the arrival of a permanent detail changes the shape of the whole operation. Schedules must be shared without being leaked, travel must be planned around advance work, and the domestic staff and the security team must learn to move through the same house without friction. The person who holds all of that together is, increasingly, the house manager.
lead.why: The estate or house manager is now expected to recruit, vet and rota a protection detail alongside the domestic staff, and to keep two very different cultures working under one roof.

articles.title: Branded residences multiply across ninety countries, and the family that buys one is really buying a household it never has to build
articles.body:
The branded residence, an apartment or villa that carries the name and the service standard of a luxury hotel or fashion house, has moved from novelty to norm. The number of live schemes worldwide has risen from 764 at the end of 2024 to around 910 by the close of 2025, a growth rate near 19 per cent in a single year. Savills projects 1,747 projects by 2032, and Knight Frank expects more than 1,000 live schemes by 2030. What was a curiosity a decade ago is now one of the most reliable growth stories in prime property.

Buyers are paying handsomely for the label. Savills calculates a global average premium of 33 per cent over an equivalent unbranded home, a figure that has held steady year on year, with resort schemes commanding an even richer 39 per cent. The premium buys more than a name over the lobby: it buys housekeeping, security, maintenance, concierge and food and beverage delivered to a hotel standard, without the owner ever having to hire or manage a soul.

The map is widening fast. The pipeline now spans more than 90 countries, with 25 of them seeing their first branded scheme. Asia Pacific has grown by 55 per cent in five years, led by Vietnam, India and Thailand, while the Middle East and North Africa have surged by 187 per cent, with Dubai at the centre of the boom. The concept, once anchored to a handful of trophy cities, is becoming a global default for the mobile wealthy.

The product itself is changing too. By 2026 luxury in these buildings is defined less by marble and more by wellbeing, with spa and wellness floors, dedicated medical services, longevity programmes and personalised fitness moving from extras to expectations. The branded residence is quietly turning into a private-service platform dressed as real estate.
articles.why: The branded residence competes directly with the traditional private household, offering hotel-grade service without in-house staff, and the estate manager must now argue the case for what a dedicated team does better.

articles.title: The explorer yacht becomes the fastest-growing hull afloat, and the crew that runs one must master the ends of the earth
articles.body:
The most telling change in the yachting market is not the size of the largest vessels but the direction of the newest ones. The expedition and explorer category is the fastest-growing cohort in the industry, and by the start of 2026 there were 101 expedition-oriented vessels in build or on order, the second-highest figure ever recorded in Boat International's Global Order Book. Projections suggest as many as 315 explorers could be delivered within a single decade by 2030.

The appeal is a shift in what wealth wants to say. For a rising generation of owners, the ostentatious superyacht anchored in central Monaco reads as a liability rather than a statement. The fastest-growing part of the fleet is not about being seen; it is about access. Luxury is increasingly defined by where a family can go, from Arctic fjords to remote Pacific atolls, rather than by what it can display along the Riviera.

These are serious machines. Explorer yachts are built for a range of 4,000 to 6,000 nautical miles or more, with enhanced stability for hard seas and expedition infrastructure that can include helicopter facilities, submersible stowage, dive centres, large tender garages and high-bandwidth satellite links. Notably, the growth is not only at the top: pocket explorers, vessels from 24 to 40 metres, now account for 72 per cent of explorer deliveries, bringing the category within reach of a far wider band of owners.

Running such a vessel is a different craft from working the Mediterranean charter circuit. Provisioning must be planned for weeks away from a chandler, medical cover must assume distance from a hospital, and the interior, increasingly built to feel like a private home rather than a floating hotel, must be maintained in conditions the conventional fleet never meets.
articles.why: Crew and shore teams on an explorer must handle remote logistics, provisioning and medical planning at range, a specialist skill set the family will pay to secure and struggle to replace.
articles.src: Impact Wealth (Boat International Global Order Book 2026)

articles.title: Monterey Car Week readies its biggest sale of the year, and the great motor car proves the collector still pays for the singular
articles.body:
Every August the collector world turns to the Monterey Peninsula for the most important few days in the global market for the motor car. The 2026 edition carries extra weight: it marks the 75th running of the Pebble Beach Concours d'Elegance, with the centrepiece staged on Sunday 16 August on the 18th fairway of Pebble Beach Golf Links at The Lodge. Around it, the great auction houses stage the year's defining sales.

The headline lot belongs to RM Sotheby's, which offers Nick Mason's 1996 McLaren F1 GTR with a presale estimate given as a value in excess of USD 35,000,000, the most expensive car on the block this year. Gooding Christie's, the official Pebble Beach partner, answers with a 1964 Shelby Cobra Daytona Coupe estimated in excess of USD 25,000,000, while a 1963 Ferrari 250 P is guided at from USD 15,000,000 to USD 20,000,000.

The field is shifting around them. Bonhams moves its sale to the Monterey Motorsports Reunion, and the theatrical presentations of Mecum and RM Sotheby's continue to draw the largest rooms. Beneath the record headline numbers, the market's message is consistent: the singular car, with unimpeachable provenance and racing history, holds its value even when the broader collectible market softens.

For the family that collects, a great motor car is not a static trophy. It travels to concours and to track, it must be stored in controlled conditions, insured to the value of a house, and documented to the last chassis number.
articles.why: A serious motor collection is a managed asset in its own right, requiring transport, climate-controlled storage, provenance records and event logistics that increasingly fall to the household to coordinate.

articles.title: The ultra-wealthy population hits a record 556,850, and the coming handover of fortunes rewrites who the household actually serves
articles.body:
The world has never held more very rich people. Altrata's World Ultra Wealth Report 2026, published on 23 June, puts the global ultra-high-net-worth population at an all-time high of 556,850 individuals, a rise of 14.4 per cent in 2025 and the strongest annual expansion since 2017. Over just two years the ranks of the ultra wealthy have grown by almost 30 per cent, adding more than 120,000 people to a group that already commands a decisive share of global assets.

The report frames the moment less as a peak than as a threshold. It identifies a USD 26 trillion investable opportunity tied to the wealth now in play, and forecasts the ultra-wealthy population to reach 746,570 individuals holding a combined USD 85 trillion by 2030. The engines of that growth are named plainly: wealth created by artificial intelligence, a reordering of global capital along geopolitical lines, and an accelerating transfer of fortunes between generations.

Geography is tilting east. Asia recorded ultra-wealthy population growth of 15.8 per cent in 2025 and is forecast to post the strongest expansion of the three major regions to 2030. New centres of demand are forming faster than the service industries that support them, which is precisely where the strain on private staffing tends to appear first.

The intergenerational handover is the part that will be felt inside the house. As fortunes pass to younger principals, the expectations of the employer change: more mobile lives, more technology, more emphasis on wellbeing and discretion, and less patience for the formality of the old household. The people who serve these families are being asked to adapt to a client who looks nothing like the one their profession was built around.
articles.why: A younger, more mobile and more tech-fluent generation of principals is inheriting the world's fortunes, and the household must evolve its manners, its systems and its skills to serve them.

articles.title: Aman opens its first Mexican resort on the Sea of Cortes, and the private-travel map gains a new coast
articles.body:
Aman, the group whose name has become shorthand for total privacy, opens its first resort in Mexico in the spring of 2026. Amanvari sits on the East Cape of Baja California Sur, where desert, farmland and shoreline meet, and it is the brand's first property with direct access to the Sea of Cortes. It is a significant addition to a map that the private traveller reads closely.

The resort occupies just 18 casitas within the 1,500-acre Costa Palmas development, and though it shares that address with a superyacht marina and a Robert Trent Jones II golf course, it operates as an independent enclave behind the wall of silence that defines the brand. The scale is deliberately small, the setting deliberately remote, and the point is seclusion within reach of serious infrastructure.

The opening lands in a demanding market. Ultra-high-net-worth travel spending rose sharply from 2023 to 2025, and that surge has left the established trophy properties under real occupancy pressure, particularly in the peak weeks. A new Aman with marina access on an underused coast offers a rare thing: a genuinely fresh option at the very top.
articles.why: The concierge and house manager who plan a family's private travel need to know a remote new Aman with its own marina, because it becomes a logistical node for a yacht itinerary as much as a place to stay.

briefs.b: Round-the-clock close protection now runs on a three-agent rota, and the salary bill alone for that cover reaches from USD 285,000 to USD 375,000 a year in the United States, before travel and equipment. It is why protection now sits on the household ledger beside the estate manager.

The branded-residence pipeline now spans more than 90 countries, with the Middle East and North Africa up 187 per cent in five years. Spa, longevity and dedicated medical services are becoming standard features rather than extras.

A 1964 Shelby Cobra Daytona Coupe carries an estimate in excess of USD 25,000,000 at Gooding Christie's Pebble Beach, the second most valuable lot of Monterey week. It trails only a 1996 McLaren F1 GTR guided above USD 35,000,000.

Amangani, Aman's clifftop lodge above Jackson Hole, has been closed for a full renovation since April 2025 and is due to reopen in late 2026. It returns to a market where trophy properties are running short of peak-season rooms.
